status_reasoning: Reviewers describe this as an 'excellent paper' that 'demonstrates the capability' of CRISPR-Cas9 to introduce targeted DSBs in human chromosomal DNA. They affirm that the authors 'advance this work by showing that Cas and guide RNAs expressed in mammalian cells can target an endogenous locus to induce DSBs,' accepting the core proof-of-concept without questioning the methodology or conclusions.

Reviewers acknowledge the efficiency data, noting that 'even if its efficiency is lower than that of competing systems, it will come to supplant ZFNs and TALE Nucleases' due to ease of programming. This indicates acceptance of the reported efficiency range and comparison to other methods, with no critique of the quantitative findings.

The reviewers do not question the lysate experiments or the conclusion that sgRNA expression/assembly is the limiting factor. These mechanistic findings are implicitly accepted as part of the overall positive assessment of the work's quality and rigor.

Reviewers note that 'they improve on the guide RNA' as one of the advances in this study. This affirms the finding that 3' extension of the sgRNA enhances targeting activity, with no concerns raised about this optimization.

Reviewers request that 'a few of the mutated targets must be sequenced (from cloned PCR products), just to demonstrate that the expected types of NHEJ mutations are present.' This indicates the sequencing data provided is insufficient for full validation, though the request is framed as confirmatory rather than corrective.

While reviewers acknowledge that 'off-target effects are an important concern for genome engineering methods,' they request the authors 'look at least at the top loci with sequence similarity to the targeting site and perform the Surveyor assay on these.' This indicates the manuscript does not adequately address off-target potential, though reviewers frame this as encouragement rather than a requirement.
